# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 46 (Bu-Vb Pc46)
**ID:** Bu-Vb Pc46
**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 46
**Title (English, from literature):** Visiting families before a meal

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Cārittasikkhāpada* (Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 46) regulates monks' visits to households in connection with an invitational meal [SuttaCentral; Vinaya Pitaka vol 4 - Mahavagga]. Under this rule, a monk who has accepted an invitation to a meal (*nimantita*) commits an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) if he calls upon lay families before or after that meal without having asked permission (*anāpucchā*) from another monk who is present, except on allowable occasions [SuttaCentral; Vinaya Pitaka vol 4 - Mahavagga; Hüsken 1997]. A recognized exception is the season for making robes, which commentary connects to the privileges of the *kaṭhina* period that allow monks to visit families without having asked leave (*anāmantacāra*) [Vinaya Pitaka vol 4 - Mahavagga; Hüsken 1997].
This training rule is widespread across Buddhist monastic traditions. Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include the Pali Bhikkhu Pātimokkha (Pc 46) and Parivāra, as well as the Pātimokkhas and Vibhaṅgas of the Sarvāstivāda (Pc 81), Mūlasarvāstivāda (Pc 81), Mahīśāsaka (Pc 82), Mahāsāṅghika (Pc 81), and Dharmaguptaka (Pc 42) traditions preserved in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan [SuttaCentral]. Corresponding rules exist for the nuns' order, including Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 127 in the Pali Canon [SuttaCentral]. In agreement with SuttaCentral's identification of a passage parallel in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6), DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali text reuse with Kd 6, the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* (Kd 16), and numerous Vibhaṅga rules concerning food and deportment (such as Pc 32, Pc 57, and Pc 33), alongside cross-language alignments with Sanskrit Prātimokṣa and Bhikṣuṇīvinaya texts and Tibetan commentaries [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
